summary.title: End-To-End Testing considered harmful
summary.one_liner: Learn why relying on many end-to-end tests conflicts with Continuous Delivery, and how a Continuous Testing strategy built on unit and acceptance tests offers faster, more deterministic feedback.
keywords: how to reduce flaky end-to-end tests
takeaways: End-to-end tests include unowned dependent services, which makes them slow, non-deterministic and hard to fix, conflicting with Continuous Delivery.
The 'Test Ice Cream Cone' (many end-to-end tests) is contrasted with the 'Test Pyramid' (many unit and acceptance tests, few end-to-end tests).
End-to-end tests should be kept for release smoke testing and production monitoring rather than build-time gating.
An end-to-end test can be pushed down the pyramid by separately checking connectivity, conversation (consumer-driven contracts) and conduct (API examples).
summary.summary: The article argues that relying heavily on end-to-end tests is incompatible with Continuous Delivery because such tests are slow, non-deterministic and span services owned by other teams. It contrasts this "Test Ice Cream Cone" approach with Continuous Testing, which uses a large base of unit and acceptance tests plus a few end-to-end tests. Using a worked Company Accounts and Payments example, it shows how the connection, conversation and conduct between services can be checked with test doubles, consumer-driven contracts and API examples. The author also links the discussion to MTTR versus MTBF, canary and blue-green releases, and chaos engineering. The second half is noted as superseded by a later talk of the same name.
